transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you. Honestly, what brings me in is that I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. It's getting really bad. Like, I'll be working, and just one saw starting up in the shop is enough to completely derail me. We've got this old Delta table saw, actually—my dad bought it back in the late 80s right before he retired. He used to build these incredible cedar chests. I still have one sitting at the foot of my bed, though my dog chewed on the bottom corner of it when he was a puppy. He's a golden retriever mix, such a good boy now, but man, those puppy years were rough on the furniture... 

Anyway, wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, work. Yeah, so a saw running, or just somebody walking past the office window, or even just me having a random thought about a different custom build... it just pulls me right off whatever I'm supposed to be doing. And then the whole day just gets away from me. I look at the clock and I've gotten absolutely nothing finished.
Are you having trouble meeting your responsibilities at work due to these distractions?

Oh, absolutely. It's... it's bad. My mistakes and just how long everything takes me now, it's actually cost me a few commissions. I had to do a complete rework on this set of built-in bookshelves last month. Which was a nightmare because the price of lumber right now—I mean, have you been to a hardware store lately? It’s outrageous. My supplier, Gary, he was saying it's all about the freight costs. Gary’s a good guy, always wears these bright red suspenders... wait, what was I saying? 

Right, the rework. So yeah, I mess up, and now the rest of the crew is just... they're a lot less willing to rely on me for scheduling the jobs or ordering materials. They'd rather just do it themselves. 

And it’s not just at the shop, honestly. At home, my husband has had to completely take over the bills and all our everyday reminders. I just keep misplacing the papers. I'll set the mail down on the kitchen island—we actually built that island together, it's a solid maple butcher block. Maple is beautiful but man, it will dull your saw blades so fast if you aren't careful. But anyway, yeah, I'd leave papers there and then just completely miss what needed to be paid or done, so he just handles all of it now.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling restless when you're not actively working on a task?

Well, yeah, I do get this... this feeling. Like if I have to sit at the desk in the office to do estimates, or if we have to sit through one of those long safety meetings the insurance company makes us do now. Which, don't get me wrong, safety is important. I actually broke my wrist a couple years ago—slipped on some sawdust near the jointer. Had to wear this heavy cast for six weeks, and it still aches when it rains. The physical therapist I saw for it, she had this amazing collection of vintage anatomy posters in her office... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, sitting still. Yeah, so during those meetings or when I'm doing estimates, I just feel so wound up inside. Like I absolutely need to get up and move around. Even though my wrist is totally healed now and I know I'm supposed to just stay put and finish the paperwork, I just... I can't stand sitting there.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?

Impulse? Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I do things without thinking. I'm usually pretty careful about my choices, especially with the business. Well, except for that time I bought that vintage lathe at an estate sale. I didn't really need it, but it was just sitting there, and the guy running the sale—he was wearing this incredible tweed jacket, the kind with the leather elbow patches. You don't see those much anymore. My grandfather used to wear one just like it when we'd go fishing up at the lake. We used to catch these huge trout... 

But no, wait, what was the question? Oh, acting on impulse. No, I don't really have a problem with that. I mean, I might get distracted and forget what I'm doing, but I don't just jump into things without thinking. I'm just... scattered, I guess.
Do you often find yourself talking excessively or interrupting others when you're with friends or family?

Talking too much? Or interrupting? No, I don't think so. I mean, my husband says I can talk his ear off sometimes, but we've been married for thirty years, so I think he's just used to it. We actually had our anniversary dinner last week at this little Italian place downtown. They make their own pasta from scratch, right there in the window. You can watch them rolling it out. The chef, he was telling us about how he imports his flour straight from Naples. Naples is supposed to be beautiful, we've always talked about taking a trip to Italy, maybe renting a villa in Tuscany... 

Wait, sorry. Interrupting people. No, I don't really do that. If anything, I'm usually the one who zones out when other people are talking. I'll just be nodding along, but my brain is completely somewhere else. So, no, I wouldn't say I talk over people or anything like that.
Do you feel anxious or overwhelmed when you're unable to focus or complete a task?

Anxious? Oh, definitely. It's awful. When I can't get something done, especially for work, my chest just gets so tight. Like last Tuesday, I was trying to finish this set of custom cabinet doors for a client. Beautiful cherry wood, really gorgeous grain on it. I had to special order it from this lumberyard two towns over because my usual guy retired. He moved down to Florida, actually. Bought a little condo near the beach. I can't imagine living in Florida with all that humidity, my hair would just be a disaster all the time, and the bugs down there... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the cabinets. So I was trying to finish them, and I just kept messing up my measurements. I'd measure it, walk over to the saw, and completely forget the number. Over and over. And I just started feeling so panicked, like I was never going to finish them, and the client was going to be furious. It gets really overwhelming, just this heavy feeling like I'm failing at everything because my brain won't cooperate.
Do you feel sad or down when you're not able to complete tasks or meet your responsibilities?

Sad? Um, I don't know if sad is the right word. Frustrated, maybe? I don't really sit around feeling down about it, I just get mad at myself. Like, why can't I just do the thing? But I wouldn't say I get depressed. I'm usually pretty upbeat. My husband always says I'm the optimist in the family. He's a bit of a worrier, always checking the weather forecast and making sure the gutters are clean. Actually, we need to clean the gutters this weekend, the oak tree in the front yard drops leaves like crazy this time of year. Last fall, we had this massive storm and the gutters got completely clogged, water was pouring over the sides like a waterfall. It completely washed out my petunias. I had just planted them, too. They were these beautiful purple ones with white stripes... 

But, uh, no. I don't really get sad or down. Just, you know, annoyed that I can't seem to keep my act together.
Do you ever find yourself so focused on a task that you lose track of everything else around you?

Focused? Like, losing track of time? No, not really. I mean, I wish I could focus like that. My brain just bounces around too much. I'll start sanding a piece of wood, and then I'll think about how I need to buy more sandpaper, which reminds me I need to go to the hardware store, and then I remember the hardware store is right next to that bakery that makes those amazing lemon bars. Have you ever had a really good lemon bar? The kind where the crust is perfectly buttery and shortbread-like, and the lemon part is actually tart, not just sweet? Most places make them way too sweet. There was this woman in my neighborhood growing up, Mrs. Gable, she made the absolute best lemon bars for the church bake sale every year. She had this huge lemon tree in her backyard, and... 

Oh, what were we talking about? Being too focused? Yeah, no, that's definitely not me. I'm usually doing five things at once and finishing none of them. I've never been one to just zero in on something and block out the world. My mind is always just buzzing away with something else.
Do you often feel restless or have trouble staying still when you're not working or engaged in an activity?

Restless? Um, well... physically, I guess I can sit in a chair, but inside? Inside I feel totally wound up. Like if I have to sit at my desk doing estimates for clients, or if I'm stuck in some long meeting with contractors... it's terrible. I just get this feeling like I need to get up and move around immediately. Even when I know I'm supposed to just stay put and finish the paperwork. 

It was really bad last year when I broke my wrist. I slipped on some ice out by my truck. It was one of those mornings where it looks wet but it's actually black ice? The worst. I went down so hard on my right hand. Had to wear this bulky cast for six weeks, which is a nightmare when you're a carpenter. I couldn't use my saws, couldn't sand anything, couldn't even hold a hammer right. My husband had to cut up my food for me at dinner, which was honestly a little humiliating. We had steak one night—he makes a really good ribeye, sears it in a cast-iron skillet with butter and rosemary. He grows the rosemary himself in these little pots on the kitchen windowsill. They smell wonderful, but they attract these tiny little fruit flies sometimes, and I've tried everything to get rid of them. Apple cider vinegar traps, sticky tape... 

But anyway, yeah. Even though my wrist is totally healed now, that wound-up feeling hasn't gone away. If I'm not actively working with my hands, I just feel like I'm crawling out of my skin wanting to move.
Are your difficulties with focus and restlessness affecting your relationships with your husband or others close to you?

Well, yeah, it definitely causes some friction. My husband, bless him, he's had to take over all the bills and the household reminders. I just kept misplacing the papers, or I'd completely forget what needed to be paid and when. I used to keep this big physical calendar on the fridge, you know, the ones with the little magnets? We had these cute little magnets shaped like different tools—a hammer, a saw, a wrench. I got them at this craft fair a few years ago. The woman making them was actually using a scroll saw to cut them out, which is pretty impressive because scroll saws can be really finicky. The blades snap so easily if you put too much pressure on them. I used to use one to make these wooden puzzles for my nieces when they were little, but then the motor burnt out and I just never got around to replacing it. 

Wait, what was I... oh, right, relationships. Yeah, so he handles all the home stuff now because I just can't keep it straight. And at work, it's honestly getting pretty bad. My mistakes and, you know, just taking too long to finish things, it's cost me commissions. I've had to redo so much work on jobs lately. The crew is getting really frustrated with me. They don't even want to rely on me for scheduling or ordering materials anymore because I always mess it up or forget something. It's just... it's embarrassing, really.
When did you first start noticing these difficulties with focus and restlessness?

Gosh, it feels like forever. Definitely even back in grade school, way before I was twelve. My teachers were always pulling my mother aside and telling her that I was bright, but just... careless. I was constantly losing my homework, or completely forgetting the instructions they had literally just given us. I'd just sit there staring out the window instead of finishing my seatwork. 

I remember my fifth-grade classroom had these huge windows that looked right out over the street, and the city was putting in a new sidewalk that year. I used to just watch the concrete guys working all afternoon. Concrete is actually really tricky to get right, you know. If the mix is too wet, it completely ruins the structural integrity, and if it's too dry, it won't cure properly and cracks over the winter. We usually sub out our concrete work on my jobs now, but I used to help pour footings when I was just starting out in the trades. It's back-breaking work, honestly. You're bent over all day with the screed board, and your boots get completely ruined. I had this one pair of Red Wing boots that I loved, took me months to break them in, and I accidentally got splatter all over them... 

Oh! Sorry. You asked when it started. But yeah, basically since I was a little girl in school, just staring out that window.
Do you experience these difficulties with focus and restlessness at home as well as at work?

Well, yeah, it's definitely not just a work thing. It's everywhere. Like, even at home when we're just trying to watch TV, or especially at church. Oh my gosh, church is the hardest. When it's supposed to be quiet and still, I just... I can't. I catch myself tapping my foot, shifting around in the pew, leaning over to whisper to my husband. Sometimes I just get up and go to the bathroom for no real reason other than I feel like I'm going to explode if I don't move. Sitting still in the quiet feels almost unbearable. 

Our church has these beautiful old wooden pews, though. Solid oak, I think. You don't see craftsmanship like that anymore. The joinery on them is incredible—they used actual mortise and tenon joints instead of just screwing everything together like they do now. I was looking at the end panels a few weeks ago and tracing the grain with my finger, and you can tell they were hand-planed. Hand-planing takes so much patience. I have this vintage Stanley No. 4 smoothing plane that I found at a flea market, and it took me three days just to restore the blade. You have to use these special water stones to get the bevel just right, and it's this whole process of working up through the grits. If you rush it, you ruin the edge, and then it just tears the wood fibers instead of slicing them clean...

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, right. Yeah, so at home, at church... pretty much anywhere I'm supposed to just sit quietly, I really struggle.
Are there any daily activities that you can still perform without significant difficulty due to your symptoms?

No, not really. I mean, it affects pretty much everything I do. Even just making breakfast or trying to organize my truck. My truck is a total disaster zone right now, actually. I drive this older Ford F-150, the one with the extended cab, and the back is just full of loose tools and half-empty boxes of screws. I was trying to find a specific box of two-inch decking screws yesterday—the ones with the star drive heads, because Phillips heads always strip out when you're driving them into pressure-treated lumber. Pressure-treated wood has gotten so expensive lately, too. We used to quote decks for half of what we have to charge now, and the chemicals they use to treat it are different since they banned the arsenic-based stuff. It eats right through regular galvanized fasteners, so you have to use the polymer-coated ones or stainless steel, which just drives the cost up even more. I had a client complain about the materials estimate last week, and I had to explain the whole chemical reaction thing to him... 

Wait, sorry, you asked about daily activities. No, honestly, I can't think of anything that isn't a struggle right now. It just bleeds into every part of my day.
Are there any parts of your daily life or relationships that haven't been affected by your difficulties with focus and restlessness?

Honestly, no. It's really taking a toll on everything. Work is getting bad. I mean, my mistakes and delays have actually cost me commissions lately. I've caused rework on jobs because I missed a measurement or forgot a detail on the plans. The crew is getting frustrated... they don't even want to rely on me for scheduling or ordering materials anymore. Which hurts, because I used to be the one who handled all the lumber orders. You really have to know your lumber grades when you're ordering, especially for finish work. Like, if you order Select or Better, you expect clear wood, but sometimes the mill slips in a few boards with knots or sapwood, and if you don't catch it before the delivery truck leaves, you're stuck with it. I had this one delivery driver, Frank, who used to try to hide the warped boards at the bottom of the stack. You always have to check the bottom of the stack. He drove this massive flatbed, an old Peterbilt, and the engine brake on that thing was so loud you could hear him coming from three blocks away...

Oh, but you asked about my life and relationships. Yeah, it's bad at home, too. My husband has basically had to take over all the bills and the calendar. I just keep misplacing the papers, or I completely miss what he tells me needs to get done. He's trying to be patient, but I know it's exhausting for him.
Do you find that you make careless mistakes on tasks or activities, such as forgetting to include important details?

Oh, constantly. It's so frustrating. I'll be doing an estimate and I just keep putting down the wrong measurements or part numbers. Like, I'll measure something as 63 inches, but my brain just flips it and I write down 36. Or I'll completely miss a line on the building permit form. And the worst part is I don't even catch it until after the lumber is already ordered and sitting on the site, or somebody on the crew has to tear out and redo the work because the cut is short. 

Which reminds me, missing that line on the permit form... man, the city permit office is a total nightmare right now. They switched to this new online portal system, but half the time it crashes, so you have to go down there in person anyway to file the paperwork. And parking downtown near the municipal building is impossible since they started that water main replacement project on 4th street. They've had the right lane closed for, like, six months. I used to do a little bit of plumbing work, mostly just rough-ins, and let me tell you, laying cast iron pipe is back-breaking. You need those special snap cutters with the chain... I bought a pair at an estate sale once from this old guy who used to work for the county. He had an incredible collection of antique pipe wrenches in his garage. Those old Ridgid wrenches, the heavy red ones, they just don't break. The teeth on the new ones wear down so fast if you're really torquing on a rusted fitting... 

Um, sorry. What was the question again? Something about careless mistakes? Yeah, the measurements and the forms... I just mess them up a lot.
Have you ever found yourself so focused on a task that you lost track of time or forgot about everything else around you?

No, not really. I mean, I don't get super focused on anything anymore. It's more like my brain is just jumping from one thing to the next, like a ping-pong ball. I used to be able to just zone in on a piece of trim work, you know, getting the miter joints perfectly tight. Coping joints is a dying art, honestly. Most guys now just throw up some caulk and paint and call it a day, but if you want a true, tight corner on crown molding, you have to cope it. I learned from this old-timer, Sal, back when I first started as an apprentice. Sal was missing half of his left index finger from a table saw accident. He always joked that it made him better at pointing out mistakes. He had this old Rockwell Unisaw, the heavy cast iron kind that took four guys to move. The motor on that thing hummed like a sewing machine... 

But yeah, no, I don't really get hyper-focused like that. I can't even stay focused long enough to finish reading an email these days.
Did you have a lot of energy or act hyper as a child?

Hyper? No, not really. I wasn't the type to be bouncing off the walls or running around the classroom or anything like that. But I definitely had problems even way back then, like, way before I was twelve. My teachers were always telling my mother the same thing at parent-teacher conferences. They'd say I was bright, but I was just so careless. I was constantly losing my homework, or I'd completely forget the instructions the teacher just gave us. I spent most of my time just staring out the window instead of finishing my seatwork. 

There was this huge oak tree outside my fourth-grade classroom window. I used to just watch the squirrels running up and down the trunk. I was obsessed with how they could just cling to the bark upside down. Bark is fascinating, really, when you think about it. It's like the tree's armor. You know, oak bark is incredibly thick and deeply grooved, which is why it's so good at surviving minor forest fires. We used to use a lot of red oak for flooring back in the day, but white oak is actually better if you're dealing with moisture because the pores are plugged up with these little growths called tyloses. That's why they use white oak for whiskey barrels. I went to a distillery once on a road trip through Kentucky, and the smell of the aging warehouses... it's this sweet, woody, vanilla smell that just sinks right into your clothes. They call the alcohol that evaporates the "angel's share." I always thought that was a beautiful way to put it. We drove my husband's old Ford Bronco on that trip, the one with the removable top. The suspension was shot, so every bump on the highway felt like you were riding a mechanical bull...

Wait, what did you ask me? About being a kid? Yeah, I wasn't hyper, just... always lost in my own world, losing my papers and staring out the window.
Have you ever been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder or ADHD by a healthcare professional?

No, I've never been diagnosed with anything like that. I mean, nobody ever really took me to a doctor for it when I was young. Back then, they didn't really test girls for that kind of stuff unless you were, you know, causing trouble. And I wasn't causing trouble, I was just... quiet. My mom always just said my head was in the clouds. 

She used to say I'd lose my head if it wasn't attached. She actually bought me this little necklace once, a silver locket, and she said it was to remind me to keep track of my things. It had a tiny little picture of our old golden retriever, Buster, inside. Buster was the best dog. He used to sleep under my dad's workbench in the garage while dad was fixing up his old Chevy truck. It was a '69 C10, stepside bed. Dad painted it this gorgeous metallic blue, but he could never get the carburetor tuned just right. It always ran a little rich, so the garage always smelled like unburnt gasoline. Honestly, I kind of love the smell of gasoline. It reminds me of summer evenings, you know? Like when you're mowing the lawn as the sun goes down and the fireflies start coming out. We used to catch them in mason jars with holes poked in the lid. You have to use a nail and a hammer to punch the holes, but if you hit it too hard, the lid bends and it won't screw back onto the glass threads properly. Glass threads are actually pretty fragile. I chipped a beautiful vintage mason jar once trying to force a bent lid onto it. It was one of those old blue glass ones from the 1920s... 

Um, but no, to answer your question, no doctor has ever told me I have that. I'm just here because I'm tired of messing up my jobs.
Did you have more energy than your peers when you were a child?

More energy? No, definitely not. Like I said, I wasn't hyper or bouncing around. If anything, I was probably less energetic than the other kids because I was always just sitting there, daydreaming. The other girls would be out playing double Dutch or tag, and I'd be sitting on the swings, just slowly dragging my feet in the dirt. 

The dirt under the swings at my elementary school was always this really fine, powdery dust. It got into everything. If you wore white canvas Keds, they were permanently gray by the end of the first week of school. My mom used to try scrubbing them with an old toothbrush and some kind of harsh bleach paste, but it never really worked. Bleach is funny like that, it breaks down the fibers in cotton if you leave it on too long. You have to be careful with it, especially if you're trying to clean up wood before you stain it. Some guys use wood bleach to take out water stains, but it can make the grain raise up, and then you have to sand it all down again anyway. Sanding is the worst part of any job. It's just hours of vibration in your hands. I have this orbital sander, a Makita, and it's a workhorse, but the dust collection bag is a joke. You end up breathing in half the sawdust anyway, which is why you're supposed to wear those N95 masks. But they fog up your safety glasses, and then you can't see the pencil line you're trying to follow...

But yeah, no. I wasn't full of energy. I was just quiet.
Do you often feel an internal restlessness or an inability to relax when you're not actively engaged in a task?

Internal restlessness? Yeah, actually. If I have to sit at the desk doing estimates for a job, or if I'm stuck sitting through a long meeting, I get this... this really wound-up feeling inside. Like I just desperately need to get up and move around. 

Estimating is the absolute worst part of the job anyway, especially lately with lumber prices bouncing all over the place. You quote a client for a custom built-in, maybe using some nice birch plywood, and by the time they finally approve the design, the price of a sheet of birch has jumped twenty bucks. Birch is really great for paint-grade cabinets, though. The grain is so tight, it doesn't telegraph through the primer like oak does. If you want to paint oak, you have to trowel on this heavy grain filler first, and that stuff smells awful. It has this weird, chalky chemical smell that reminds me of the drywall joint compound we used to use back in the 90s before they changed the formula. That old mud used to dry so hard you practically needed an angle grinder to sand it smooth, and the dust would just coat the entire house. You'd be blowing white dust out of your nose for a week...

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right, sitting at the desk. Yeah, even though my wrist is totally healed now and I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish up the paperwork, I just feel completely wound up and tense if I'm not actively doing something with my hands.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about talking excessively or interrupting others, which correspond to hyperactive/impulsive symptoms like 'Talking excessively' or 'Interrupting/intruding'. My symptom profile does not include these symptoms.

patient.answer:
Talking too much? Or interrupting? No, I don't think so. I mean, my husband says I can talk his ear off sometimes, but we've been married for thirty years, so I think he's just used to it. We actually had our anniversary dinner last week at this little Italian place downtown. They make their own pasta from scratch, right there in the window. You can watch them rolling it out. The chef, he was telling us about how he imports his flour straight from Naples. Naples is supposed to be beautiful, we've always talked about taking a trip to Italy, maybe renting a villa in Tuscany... 

Wait, sorry. Interrupting people. No, I don't really do that. If anything, I'm usually the one who zones out when other people are talking. I'll just be nodding along, but my brain is completely somewhere else. So, no, I wouldn't say I talk over people or anything like that.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are associated with emotional distress
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or overwhelmed when you're unable to focus or complete a task?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling anxious or overwhelmed when unable to focus or complete a task, which relates to anxiety or emotional regulation. None of my symptom profiles specifically cover anxiety or feeling overwhelmed due to inability to focus.

patient.answer:
Anxious? Oh, definitely. It's awful. When I can't get something done, especially for work, my chest just gets so tight. Like last Tuesday, I was trying to finish this set of custom cabinet doors for a client. Beautiful cherry wood, really gorgeous grain on it. I had to special order it from this lumberyard two towns over because my usual guy retired. He moved down to Florida, actually. Bought a little condo near the beach. I can't imagine living in Florida with all that humidity, my hair would just be a disaster all the time, and the bugs down there... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the cabinets. So I was trying to finish them, and I just kept messing up my measurements. I'd measure it, walk over to the saw, and completely forget the number. Over and over. And I just started feeling so panicked, like I was never going to finish them, and the client was going to be furious. It gets really overwhelming, just this heavy feeling like I'm failing at everything because my brain won't cooperate.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are associated with emotional distress
doctor.question: Do you feel sad or down when you're not able to complete tasks or meet your responsibilities?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling sad or down (depressive symptoms) in relation to task incompletion, which is not covered in my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Sad? Um, I don't know if sad is the right word. Frustrated, maybe? I don't really sit around feeling down about it, I just get mad at myself. Like, why can't I just do the thing? But I wouldn't say I get depressed. I'm usually pretty upbeat. My husband always says I'm the optimist in the family. He's a bit of a worrier, always checking the weather forecast and making sure the gutters are clean. Actually, we need to clean the gutters this weekend, the oak tree in the front yard drops leaves like crazy this time of year. Last fall, we had this massive storm and the gutters got completely clogged, water was pouring over the sides like a waterfall. It completely washed out my petunias. I had just planted them, too. They were these beautiful purple ones with white stripes... 

But, uh, no. I don't really get sad or down. Just, you know, annoyed that I can't seem to keep my act together.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of hyperfocus
doctor.question: Do you ever find yourself so focused on a task that you lose track of everything else around you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hyperfocus (being so focused on a task that you lose track of everything else), which is not listed in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Focused? Like, losing track of time? No, not really. I mean, I wish I could focus like that. My brain just bounces around too much. I'll start sanding a piece of wood, and then I'll think about how I need to buy more sandpaper, which reminds me I need to go to the hardware store, and then I remember the hardware store is right next to that bakery that makes those amazing lemon bars. Have you ever had a really good lemon bar? The kind where the crust is perfectly buttery and shortbread-like, and the lemon part is actually tart, not just sweet? Most places make them way too sweet. There was this woman in my neighborhood growing up, Mrs. Gable, she made the absolute best lemon bars for the church bake sale every year. She had this huge lemon tree in her backyard, and... 

Oh, what were we talking about? Being too focused? Yeah, no, that's definitely not me. I'm usually doing five things at once and finishing none of them. I've never been one to just zero in on something and block out the world. My mind is always just buzzing away with something else.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of hyperactivity in daily life
doctor.question: Do you often feel restless or have trouble staying still when you're not working or engaged in an activity?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: If I have to sit at the desk doing estimates or sit through a long meeting, I feel wound up inside like I need to get up and move around, even though my wrist is healed and I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I often feel restless or have trouble staying still, which maps directly to the 'Feeling_Restless' symptom.

patient.answer:
Restless? Um, well... physically, I guess I can sit in a chair, but inside? Inside I feel totally wound up. Like if I have to sit at my desk doing estimates for clients, or if I'm stuck in some long meeting with contractors... it's terrible. I just get this feeling like I need to get up and move around immediately. Even when I know I'm supposed to just stay put and finish the paperwork. 

It was really bad last year when I broke my wrist. I slipped on some ice out by my truck. It was one of those mornings where it looks wet but it's actually black ice? The worst. I went down so hard on my right hand. Had to wear this bulky cast for six weeks, which is a nightmare when you're a carpenter. I couldn't use my saws, couldn't sand anything, couldn't even hold a hammer right. My husband had to cut up my food for me at dinner, which was honestly a little humiliating. We had steak one night—he makes a really good ribeye, sears it in a cast-iron skillet with butter and rosemary. He grows the rosemary himself in these little pots on the kitchen windowsill. They smell wonderful, but they attract these tiny little fruit flies sometimes, and I've tried everything to get rid of them. Apple cider vinegar traps, sticky tape... 

But anyway, yeah. Even though my wrist is totally healed now, that wound-up feeling hasn't gone away. If I'm not actively working with my hands, I just feel like I'm crawling out of my skin wanting to move.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting their daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Are your difficulties with focus and restlessness affecting your relationships with your husband or others close to you?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My mistakes and delays have cost me commissions, caused rework on jobs, and made the crew less willing to rely on me for scheduling or ordering. At home, my husband has had to take over bills and reminders because I keep misplacing papers or missing what needs to be done.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how the symptoms are affecting my relationships and daily life, which corresponds to the functional impairment criterion.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, it definitely causes some friction. My husband, bless him, he's had to take over all the bills and the household reminders. I just kept misplacing the papers, or I'd completely forget what needed to be paid and when. I used to keep this big physical calendar on the fridge, you know, the ones with the little magnets? We had these cute little magnets shaped like different tools—a hammer, a saw, a wrench. I got them at this craft fair a few years ago. The woman making them was actually using a scroll saw to cut them out, which is pretty impressive because scroll saws can be really finicky. The blades snap so easily if you put too much pressure on them. I used to use one to make these wooden puzzles for my nieces when they were little, but then the motor burnt out and I just never got around to replacing it. 

Wait, what was I... oh, right, relationships. Yeah, so he handles all the home stuff now because I just can't keep it straight. And at work, it's honestly getting pretty bad. My mistakes and, you know, just taking too long to finish things, it's cost me commissions. I've had to redo so much work on jobs lately. The crew is getting really frustrated with me. They don't even want to rely on me for scheduling or ordering materials anymore because I always mess it up or forget something. It's just... it's embarrassing, really.

doctor.intent: Determine the age of onset for the patient's symptoms
doctor.question: When did you first start noticing these difficulties with focus and restlessness?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even back in grade school, before I was 12, teachers were always telling my mother I was bright but careless, losing homework, forgetting instructions, and staring out the window instead of finishing my seatwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the initial onset of the symptoms ('first start noticing'), which maps to the criterion regarding symptom onset prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Gosh, it feels like forever. Definitely even back in grade school, way before I was twelve. My teachers were always pulling my mother aside and telling her that I was bright, but just... careless. I was constantly losing my homework, or completely forgetting the instructions they had literally just given us. I'd just sit there staring out the window instead of finishing my seatwork. 

I remember my fifth-grade classroom had these huge windows that looked right out over the street, and the city was putting in a new sidewalk that year. I used to just watch the concrete guys working all afternoon. Concrete is actually really tricky to get right, you know. If the mix is too wet, it completely ruins the structural integrity, and if it's too dry, it won't cure properly and cracks over the winter. We usually sub out our concrete work on my jobs now, but I used to help pour footings when I was just starting out in the trades. It's back-breaking work, honestly. You're bent over all day with the screed board, and your boots get completely ruined. I had this one pair of Red Wing boots that I loved, took me months to break them in, and I accidentally got splatter all over them... 

Oh! Sorry. You asked when it started. But yeah, basically since I was a little girl in school, just staring out that window.

doctor.intent: determine if symptoms are persistent across situations
doctor.question: Do you experience these difficulties with focus and restlessness at home as well as at work?

target_item.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: Even at home or in church, when things are supposed to be quiet, I catch myself tapping, shifting around, whispering to my husband, or getting up for no real reason because sitting still in the quiet feels almost unbearable.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the restlessness occurs at home as well, which aligns with the patient's difficulty engaging in quiet leisure activities at home or church.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, it's definitely not just a work thing. It's everywhere. Like, even at home when we're just trying to watch TV, or especially at church. Oh my gosh, church is the hardest. When it's supposed to be quiet and still, I just... I can't. I catch myself tapping my foot, shifting around in the pew, leaning over to whisper to my husband. Sometimes I just get up and go to the bathroom for no real reason other than I feel like I'm going to explode if I don't move. Sitting still in the quiet feels almost unbearable. 

Our church has these beautiful old wooden pews, though. Solid oak, I think. You don't see craftsmanship like that anymore. The joinery on them is incredible—they used actual mortise and tenon joints instead of just screwing everything together like they do now. I was looking at the end panels a few weeks ago and tracing the grain with my finger, and you can tell they were hand-planed. Hand-planing takes so much patience. I have this vintage Stanley No. 4 smoothing plane that I found at a flea market, and it took me three days just to restore the blade. You have to use these special water stones to get the bevel just right, and it's this whole process of working up through the grits. If you rush it, you ruin the edge, and then it just tears the wood fibers instead of slicing them clean...

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, right. Yeah, so at home, at church... pretty much anywhere I'm supposed to just sit quietly, I really struggle.

No, not really. I mean, it affects pretty much everything I do. Even just making breakfast or trying to organize my truck. My truck is a total disaster zone right now, actually. I drive this older Ford F-150, the one with the extended cab, and the back is just full of loose tools and half-empty boxes of screws. I was trying to find a specific box of two-inch decking screws yesterday—the ones with the star drive heads, because Phillips heads always strip out when you're driving them into pressure-treated lumber. Pressure-treated wood has gotten so expensive lately, too. We used to quote decks for half of what we have to charge now, and the chemicals they use to treat it are different since they banned the arsenic-based stuff. It eats right through regular galvanized fasteners, so you have to use the polymer-coated ones or stainless steel, which just drives the cost up even more. I had a client complain about the materials estimate last week, and I had to explain the whole chemical reaction thing to him... 

Wait, sorry, you asked about daily activities. No, honestly, I can't think of anything that isn't a struggle right now. It just bleeds into every part of my day.

I had this one delivery driver, Frank, who used to try to hide the warped boards at the bottom of the stack. You always have to check the bottom of the stack. doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are consistent with a pattern of inattention that is more typical of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

patient.answer:
Oh, constantly. It's so frustrating. I'll be doing an estimate and I just keep putting down the wrong measurements or part numbers. Like, I'll measure something as 63 inches, but my brain just flips it and I write down 36. Or I'll completely miss a line on the building permit form. And the worst part is I don't even catch it until after the lumber is already ordered and sitting on the site, or somebody on the crew has to tear out and redo the work because the cut is short. 

Which reminds me, missing that line on the permit form... man, the city permit office is a total nightmare right now. They switched to this new online portal system, but half the time it crashes, so you have to go down there in person anyway to file the paperwork. And parking downtown near the municipal building is impossible since they started that water main replacement project on 4th street. They've had the right lane closed for, like, six months. I used to do a little bit of plumbing work, mostly just rough-ins, and let me tell you, laying cast iron pipe is back-breaking. You need those special snap cutters with the chain... I bought a pair at an estate sale once from this old guy who used to work for the county. He had an incredible collection of antique pipe wrenches in his garage. Those old Ridgid wrenches, the heavy red ones, they just don't break. The teeth on the new ones wear down so fast if you're really torquing on a rusted fitting... 

Um, sorry. What was the question again? Something about careless mistakes? Yeah, the measurements and the forms... I just mess them up a lot.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of hyperfocus
doctor.question: Have you ever found yourself so focused on a task that you lost track of time or forgot about everything else around you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hyperfocus (losing track of time due to intense focus on a task), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I mean, I don't get super focused on anything anymore. It's more like my brain is just jumping from one thing to the next, like a ping-pong ball. I used to be able to just zone in on a piece of trim work, you know, getting the miter joints perfectly tight. Coping joints is a dying art, honestly. Most guys now just throw up some caulk and paint and call it a day, but if you want a true, tight corner on crown molding, you have to cope it. I learned from this old-timer, Sal, back when I first started as an apprentice. Sal was missing half of his left index finger from a table saw accident. He always joked that it made him better at pointing out mistakes. He had this old Rockwell Unisaw, the heavy cast iron kind that took four guys to move. The motor on that thing hummed like a sewing machine... 

But yeah, no, I don't really get hyper-focused like that. I can't even stay focused long enough to finish reading an email these days.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of hyperactivity in childhood
doctor.question: Did you have a lot of energy or act hyper as a child?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even back in grade school, before I was 12, teachers were always telling my mother I was bright but careless, losing homework, forgetting instructions, and staring out the window instead of finishing my seatwork.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about childhood symptoms (hyperactivity/energy), which maps to the requirement of symptom onset prior to age 12. I will use this item to explain what my symptoms were actually like during childhood.

patient.answer:
Hyper? No, not really. I wasn't the type to be bouncing off the walls or running around the classroom or anything like that. But I definitely had problems even way back then, like, way before I was twelve. My teachers were always telling my mother the same thing at parent-teacher conferences. They'd say I was bright, but I was just so careless. I was constantly losing my homework, or I'd completely forget the instructions the teacher just gave us. I spent most of my time just staring out the window instead of finishing my seatwork. 

There was this huge oak tree outside my fourth-grade classroom window. I used to just watch the squirrels running up and down the trunk. I was obsessed with how they could just cling to the bark upside down. Bark is fascinating, really, when you think about it. It's like the tree's armor. You know, oak bark is incredibly thick and deeply grooved, which is why it's so good at surviving minor forest fires. We used to use a lot of red oak for flooring back in the day, but white oak is actually better if you're dealing with moisture because the pores are plugged up with these little growths called tyloses. That's why they use white oak for whiskey barrels. I went to a distillery once on a road trip through Kentucky, and the smell of the aging warehouses... it's this sweet, woody, vanilla smell that just sinks right into your clothes. They call the alcohol that evaporates the "angel's share." I always thought that was a beautiful way to put it. We drove my husband's old Ford Bronco on that trip, the one with the removable top. The suspension was shot, so every bump on the highway felt like you were riding a mechanical bull...

Wait, what did you ask me? About being a kid? Yeah, I wasn't hyper, just... always lost in my own world, losing my papers and staring out the window.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are consistent with a pattern of inattention and impulsivity that is more typical of ADHD
doctor.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder or ADHD by a healthcare professional?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a previous formal diagnosis of ADHD, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I've never been diagnosed with anything like that. I mean, nobody ever really took me to a doctor for it when I was young. Back then, they didn't really test girls for that kind of stuff unless you were, you know, causing trouble. And I wasn't causing trouble, I was just... quiet. My mom always just said my head was in the clouds. 

She used to say I'd lose my head if it wasn't attached. She actually bought me this little necklace once, a silver locket, and she said it was to remind me to keep track of my things. It had a tiny little picture of our old golden retriever, Buster, inside. Buster was the best dog. He used to sleep under my dad's workbench in the garage while dad was fixing up his old Chevy truck. It was a '69 C10, stepside bed. Dad painted it this gorgeous metallic blue, but he could never get the carburetor tuned just right. It always ran a little rich, so the garage always smelled like unburnt gasoline. Honestly, I kind of love the smell of gasoline. It reminds me of summer evenings, you know? Like when you're mowing the lawn as the sun goes down and the fireflies start coming out. We used to catch them in mason jars with holes poked in the lid. You have to use a nail and a hammer to punch the holes, but if you hit it too hard, the lid bends and it won't screw back onto the glass threads properly. Glass threads are actually pretty fragile. I chipped a beautiful vintage mason jar once trying to force a bent lid onto it. It was one of those old blue glass ones from the 1920s... 

Um, but no, to answer your question, no doctor has ever told me I have that. I'm just here because I'm tired of messing up my jobs.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of hyperactivity in childhood
doctor.question: Did you have more energy than your peers when you were a child?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about having more energy than peers during childhood (childhood hyperactivity). The patient's symptom profile does not include childhood hyperactivity; the only childhood onset symptom noted is inattention.

patient.answer:
More energy? No, definitely not. Like I said, I wasn't hyper or bouncing around. If anything, I was probably less energetic than the other kids because I was always just sitting there, daydreaming. The other girls would be out playing double Dutch or tag, and I'd be sitting on the swings, just slowly dragging my feet in the dirt. 

The dirt under the swings at my elementary school was always this really fine, powdery dust. It got into everything. If you wore white canvas Keds, they were permanently gray by the end of the first week of school. My mom used to try scrubbing them with an old toothbrush and some kind of harsh bleach paste, but it never really worked. Bleach is funny like that, it breaks down the fibers in cotton if you leave it on too long. You have to be careful with it, especially if you're trying to clean up wood before you stain it. Some guys use wood bleach to take out water stains, but it can make the grain raise up, and then you have to sand it all down again anyway. Sanding is the worst part of any job. It's just hours of vibration in your hands. I have this orbital sander, a Makita, and it's a workhorse, but the dust collection bag is a joke. You end up breathing in half the sawdust anyway, which is why you're supposed to wear those N95 masks. But they fog up your safety glasses, and then you can't see the pencil line you're trying to follow...

But yeah, no. I wasn't full of energy. I was just quiet.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of hyperactivity in adulthood
doctor.question: Do you often feel an internal restlessness or an inability to relax when you're not actively engaged in a task?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: If I have to sit at the desk doing estimates or sit through a long meeting, I feel wound up inside like I need to get up and move around, even though my wrist is healed and I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about internal restlessness, which directly matches the symptom of feeling restless.

patient.answer:
Internal restlessness? Yeah, actually. If I have to sit at the desk doing estimates for a job, or if I'm stuck sitting through a long meeting, I get this... this really wound-up feeling inside. Like I just desperately need to get up and move around. 

Estimating is the absolute worst part of the job anyway, especially lately with lumber prices bouncing all over the place. You quote a client for a custom built-in, maybe using some nice birch plywood, and by the time they finally approve the design, the price of a sheet of birch has jumped twenty bucks. Birch is really great for paint-grade cabinets, though. The grain is so tight, it doesn't telegraph through the primer like oak does. If you want to paint oak, you have to trowel on this heavy grain filler first, and that stuff smells awful. It has this weird, chalky chemical smell that reminds me of the drywall joint compound we used to use back in the 90s before they changed the formula. That old mud used to dry so hard you practically needed an angle grinder to sand it smooth, and the dust would just coat the entire house. You'd be blowing white dust out of your nose for a week...

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right, sitting at the desk. Yeah, even though my wrist is totally healed now and I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish up the paperwork, I just feel completely wound up and tense if I'm not actively doing something with my hands.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?
